pr_title: Do not clear state of pods pending admission for CPU/Memory/Device manager
pr_body:

/kind bug
/kind regression

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Do not remove admitted pods from the state until the pod passed the admission phase.

- [x] CPU manager
- [x] Memory manager
- [x] Device manager

issue_context.title: The CPU manager does not work correctly for the guaranteed pod with multiple containers
issue_context.body:
#### What happened:

The CPU manager removes the allocation for previous containers under the guaranteed pod once the next container allocation started.

The CPU manager test fails because of it
```
E2eNode Suite: [sig-node] CPU Manager [Serial] [Feature:CPUManager] With kubeconfig updated with static CPU Manager policy run the CPU Manager tests should assign CPUs as expected based on the Pod spec
```
https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-jenkins/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-cpu-manager/1420014879246389248

#### What you expected to happen:

The CPU manager should keep previous containers allocations.

#### How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible):

- Start the guaranteed pod with two containers
- Verify the CPU pining for the first container

#### Anything else we need to know?:

I think the problem introduced by recent refactor under https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/3eadd1a9ead7a009a9abfbd603a5efd0560473cc

Issue is urgent but **not** release blocking this late: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1627409859207800?thread_ts=1627408015.203100&cid=C0BP8PW9G

Confirmed CPU manager e2e has been failing since 07/08 which is when Clayton's refactor initially landed: https://prow.k8s.io/job-history/gs/kubernetes-jenkins/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-cpu-manager?buildId=1413362483304861696

I commented on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/103953#issuecomment-887856835 but I'm pretty sure the code here was wrong before my change - a pod in admission cannot be in `GetActivePods()` until it's actually delivered to the pod worker, so any background process you run that refreshes the pod worker has to track that.

I noticed that the cpu manager periodically reconciles - this is not synchronized with pod configuration management, so this call can race with the pod config loop (the pod shows up, is checked for admission, and then reconcileState() runs before the pod is added to the pod worker).

```
	// Periodically call m.reconcileState() to continue to keep the CPU sets of
	// all pods in sync with and guaranteed CPUs handed out among them.
	go wait.Until(func() { m.reconcileState() }, m.reconcilePeriod, wait.NeverStop)
```

A pod is not an active pod until it is passed to a pod worker.  Anyone relying on the behavior before (prior to my change) was accidentally including pods that are not active (because the bug #102344 fixed was that pods were incorrectly listed as active).

You either need to ensure reconcile is only called during pod housekeeping (which is synchronized with the config loop) or your cpu manager needs to track pods that are "in flight for admission but not yet active" (kube apiserver admission quota does this).
Thanks for the info. Probably the second is the best option for us.
it seems the device manager (as well as the memory manager) can hit the same issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.21/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L621

> Issue is urgent but **not** release blocking this late: https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C0BP8PW9G/p1627409859207800?thread_ts=1627408015.203100&cid=C0BP8PW9G
> 
> Confirmed CPU manager e2e has been failing since 07/08 which is when Clayton's refactor initially landed: https://prow.k8s.io/job-history/gs/kubernetes-jenkins/logs/ci-kubernetes-node-kubelet-serial-cpu-manager?buildId=1413362483304861696

A bit more context: turns out all the resource managers (cpu, memory, device) use the same core logic, so in addition to the cpu manager we are tracking here, the memory manager is surely broken as well, and [the device manager](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.21/pkg/kubelet/cm/devicemanager/manager.go#L621) is almost certainly (= same logic but no test to prove the breakage atm) broken as well

Digging into this more, I see the problem and why it started breaking.  

> Admission plugins should not be using GetActivePods() to check the state of "all known pods" if they are tracking admitted requests, because GetActivePods() is post admission

To be broken, an admission handler must store data in internal maps AND have a background loop that checks GetActivePods (please verify who is impacted)

## Problem

There are two sets of pods in the Kubelet:

1. Those that are in config (in one or more of the config sources at the current time)
2. Those that are recognized by the Kubelet to do work (owned by the pod worker)

These are mostly overlapping groups:

```
|----------------------------------|            (config)      <- in the podManager.GetPods()
         |------------------------------------| (pod worker)  <- passed admission AND in the podWorker
         |------------------------------|       (active)      <- kubelet.GetActivePods() after my change
|--------|                                             (pod not yet admitted)
```

The bug that my change fixed was that some components were assuming that the first set and the second set are the same, especially cleanup loops.  My change however impacted GetActivePods to the majority definition, which is correct for admission (kubelet) but not for the cleanup loops inside admission handler components (which are assuming that admission cannot fail).

Any admission plugin that "allocates" internal resources needs to track the difference between a resource request (created in admission) and an actual reserved resource (for a pod that has passed admission and is known to the pod worker).  It appears if most of our admission plugins are assuming that all admission succeeds by simply allocating and then cleaning up later, which is incorrect if admission fails.  Admission that resyncs the state of the internal manager from a list of valid pods before it performs an Admit check can work around part of this (like cpu manager) by changing the list of pods it acts on.

## Other possible fixes

At least for the cpu manager, it needs to get the list of active pods AND then conditionally include the current pod.  The list of GetActivePods is already passed to the admission handler, and the admission hook can use that to check whether the pod is "already admitted" or not.  We should never invoke the admission handler twice (for each container), so that sounds like an admission handler bug if you are cleaning up your internal state in the middle of a single `Admit` call.

@smarterclayton thanks for the clear description of the issue. I believe that the proposal you have in "Other possible fixes" is the one that we should take for these components.

@fromanirh @cynepco3hahue please assign me to the PR you put together to fix this.

review_comments:
I think this is only partially correct.  You need to prune the admitted pods map to only include those that are still in either config or pod worker but not in both (a pod that is in the pod worker is by definition admitted).  You also want to exclude pods that are no longer running due to termination (which means we will never start the container again, thus we can reuse those CPUs).  You then need to take that pruned list of admitted pods and add it to active pods to get the list of "pods that should be considered to be allocated guaranteed resources"

I think we'll need to add a method on kubelet to make this easier - looking at what that would be right now.

Looking at this, I think we have a bug in that these components need to know about pods that are terminating that have been force deleted (which activePods() does not include).  @Random-Liu I think that components like the cpu_manager, memory_manager, qos_container_manager, and device_manager actually need to know pods that have been force deleted but are still running.  To do that, I'm going to need to enable the pod worker to share that info safely (and consistently, i think).

I'm not sure what you suggest here is necessary. As you mentioned in your comment [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/103952#issuecomment-888387811), all we should really need to care about is whether the pod is:

(1) in the active pods list; or
(2) some pod currently waiting to be admitted

Assuming logic exists to _atomically_ add an admitted pod to the active pod list before starting the next iteration of the admission loop, I believe this should be sufficient. If it doesn't make it into the active list, then we shouldn't be tracking it anyway, and if it's ever removed from the list, we should be done tracking it.

We just then need to track a single variable to hold the "currently being admitting" pod that gets overwritten each time a new iteration of the admit loop starts.

The check in `removeStaleState()` would then remove any state not currently associated with a pod in the active list + this new variable.

Of course this is all contingent on what I said before:
> Assuming logic exists to _atomically_ add an admitted pod to the active pod list before starting the next iteration of the admission loop, I believe this should be sufficient.

Maybe there's good reason not to do this?

> (1) in the active pods list; or

The bug is that the active pods list does not include force deleted pods that may take tens of minutes to complete that may still have running containers that are pinned to certain CPUs.
Is that a problem though? I would think we can safely remove the CPUs assigned to them then, and the next time around the reconcile loop, their containers will be moved onto non-exclusive CPUs.
Ah, nevermind, the reconcile loop also relies on the activePods List, so there is no way to know we should move these deleted pods to non-exclusive CPUs.

On thing to consider here -- while I agree that this would be nice to have -- it's not something we supported before, so not including it now would not be a regression. It should be in it's own PR.

I also still think there's a way to handle this without adding a new function (i.e. track which pods' state was removed from `removeStaleState()` and check each of it's container statuses one last time the next time it is in the reconcile loop). If any of them are still running, it will trigger the `Update()` call at the bottom of the loop to remove it's exclusive CPUs.

@smarterclayton Do you know if the `GetActivePods()` returned force deleted pods before the refactoring? If no, for now, we can at least fix the code to have old behavior and once we will have an option to get force deleted pods, we can refactor the code again.

It doesn’t matter if it included these pods or not before — we’ve never had logic to actually call ‚update()‘ on the containers associated with these types of pods to remove CPUs  from them if they were still running. That is the new logic we would need to add.

Although, I guess if activePods() used to include terminated (but still running) pods before, then we never would have removed stale state about them here, making us „think“ their CPUs were free (even though containers are still running on them).

> Although, I guess if activePods() used to include terminated (but still running) pods before, then we never would have removed stale state about them here, making us „think“ their CPUs were free (even though containers are still running on them).

AFAIU/CT this is the most pressing question now. I fully agree about the general idea to restore the old (and, we learned, not covering some important cases) behaviour and iterating later to actually cover them. The former is important and urgent, the later important as well but less urgent.
ActivePods() never returned pods that were force deleted.  So you have always been broken on that.
In this case, can we restore at least the old behavior under the current PR, and once we will have the infrastructure to get force deleted pods we can improve the logic under resource managers.
I opened an issue to monitor force deleted pods problem - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/104099
I agree this does not block this change, and probably the fix for 104099 should make the code changes here simpler (but we don't have to do it now).
